|�​(B)k→⟩=∑x→ei​k→​x→​|�​(B)x→⟩.\displaystyle\ket{\phi(B)_{\vec{k}}}=\sum_{\vec{x}}\mathrm{e}^{i\vec{k}\vec{x}}\ket{\phi(B)_{\vec{x}}}. (25)

The coefficients of tensor BB are then determined by energy minimisation of the excited state, for which AD can again be used [42, 132]. In contrast to the regular ground state optimisation, here the CTMRG routine must be extended to include the appropriate phase factors in the directional absorption. Moreover, instead of only eight environment tensors per iPEPS tensor in the unit cell, the action of BB, B†B^{\dagger} and the product of BB and B†B^{\dagger} has to be tracked in three additional sets of eight tensors.

The excited state approach can be directly extended to different lattice geometries. To this end, we have to generalize the absorption of iPEPS tensors (growing the CTMRG transfer tensors T1T_{1}, T2T_{2}, T3T_{3} and T4T_{4}) to include the basis of the lattice, respecting relative phase factors of the basis vectors. Depending on the actual structure of the basis, a separate tensor BnB_{n} is chosen as a perturbation for each of the basis site. Our implementation already contains the main building blocks of a robust and flexible CTMRG routine, calculation of gradients using AD at the fixed-point and minimisation of an energy cost function. The extension of the framework to include excited states is therefore natural. It is planned as a future feature.

4.7 Comments on fermionic systems

As a final comment we stress that for clarity and to be concise, we have focused in our presentation on quantum spin models. It should be clear, however, that the machinery developed here readily carries over to the study of interacting fermionic systems, with little modifications. Naively, one might think that the simulation of two-dimensional fermionic models is marred by substantial overheads that emerge when invoking a spin-to-fermion mapping. This is, however, not the case, and the respective book-keeping of the signs can be done with negligible overhead [133, 134]. On the formal level, such tensor networks involve a particular choice of what is called a spin structure [135, 136]. Practically speaking, one can modify much of the bosonic code for PEPS to the fermionic setting, readily incorporating the relevant signs to capture interacting fermions, in what is called fermionic PEPS [133, 137, 138]. This insight is important as some of the most compelling test cases of interacting quantum many-body systems are of a fermionic nature.

5 Conclusion and prospects

In this review we present a comprehensive introduction into automatic differentiation in the context of two-dimensional tensor networks, leading to the recently emerging variational iPEPS framework for ground state optimization. We provide implementation details and discuss obstacles that arise in practice, as well as techniques to mitigate these. At the same time, we coherently present ideas that have to date only been mentioned in a fragmented fashion in the literature. We hope that the present work can serve as a useful reference and review in the variational study of 2d tensor networks.

This work accompanies the variational iPEPS library variPEPS, a comprehensive and versatile code base for optimizing iPEPS in a general setting. We expect this library to be a helpful tool for performing state-of-the-art tensor network analyses for a wide range of physical models, featuring multiple two-dimensional lattices. The library is designed to be extended with additional simulation techniques based on automatic differentiation, such as excited states and structure factors.

The variPEPS library is publicly available in both a Julia and a Python version on GitHub [56], with stable references in the corresponding Zenodo repositories [58, 57].

Appendix: Background on automatic differentiation

Appendix A Adjoint functions and variables

In the literature it is common to use so called adjoint functions and adjoint variables when using backwards-mode AD. These adjoint functions map the adjoint variables onto each other, as in Eq. (16) when building up the gradient. In this section, we will briefly introduce the basic notation of adjoint functions and variables following Ref. [145]. Explicit constructions of adjoint functions, which are vector-Jacobian-products in the practical implementation, for a large number of useful operations including those for the iPEPS use-case can be found in Refs. [145, 146, 147].

As an example throughout this section, we consider the function hh, composed out of two primitive functions h1h_{1} and h2h_{2} which are concatenated as

h=h2∘h1,h1:Mn×n×Mn×n→Mn×n,h2:Mn×n→R,\begin{split}h&=h_{2}\circ h_{1},\\ h_{1}&:M_{n\times n}\times M_{n\times n}\xrightarrow{}M_{n\times n},\\ h_{2}&:M_{n\times n}\xrightarrow{}\mdmathbb{R},\end{split} (A.1)

with variables (A,B)∈Mn×n×Mn×n(A,B)\in M_{n\times n}\times M_{n\times n}, C∈Mn×nC\in M_{n\times n} and x∈Rx\in\mdmathbb{R}. We start by examining the differential of the output variable xx

d​x=∂h2∂C​d​C=:∑i,jC¯i,j​d​Ci,j=Tr⁡(C¯𝖳​d​C).dx=\frac{\partial h_{2}}{\partial C}dC=:\sum_{i,j}\bar{C}_{i,j}dC_{i,j}=\mathrm{Tr}(\bar{C}^{\mkern-1.5mu\mathsf{T}}dC). (A.2)

In the first equation, we have suppressed the sum over the indices of CC. Eq. (A.2) defines the adjoint variable C¯\bar{C} of CC. We see that the adjoint variable C¯\bar{C} is the derivative of the scalar output of the function h2h_{2} w.r.t. CC. Thus, for the case of a scalar output the variable CC and the adjoint variable C¯\bar{C} have the same dimension. Now, in order to get the gradient ∇h\nabla h we are interested in the derivative of the output w.r.t. the input variables (A,B)(A,B). To this end we consider the differential of the intermediate variable

d​C=∂h1∂A​d​A+∂h1∂B​d​B.\displaystyle dC=\frac{\partial h_{1}}{\partial A}dA+\frac{\partial h_{1}}{\partial B}dB. (A.3)

Inserting this into Eq. (A.2), we obtain

d​x=Tr⁡(C¯𝖳​∂h1∂A⏟A¯𝖳​d​A)+Tr⁡(C¯𝖳​∂h1∂B⏟B¯𝖳​d​B).dx=\mathrm{Tr}\bigg(\underbrace{\bar{C}^{\mkern-1.5mu\mathsf{T}}\frac{\partial h_{1}}{\partial A}}_{\bar{A}^{\mkern-1.5mu\mathsf{T}}}dA\bigg)+\mathrm{Tr}\bigg(\underbrace{\bar{C}^{\mkern-1.5mu\mathsf{T}}\frac{\partial h_{1}}{\partial B}}_{\bar{B}^{\mkern-1.5mu\mathsf{T}}}dB\bigg). (A.4)

Here we have already implicitly used the adjoint function h¯1\bar{h}_{1} that maps the adjoint variable C¯\bar{C} to the adjoint variables A¯\bar{A} and B¯\bar{B} according to

h¯1:C¯𝖳↦(A¯𝖳,B¯𝖳)𝖳=(C¯𝖳​∂h1∂A,C¯𝖳​∂h1∂B)𝖳.\bar{h}_{1}:\bar{C}^{\mkern-1.5mu\mathsf{T}}\xmapsto{}(\bar{A}^{\mkern-1.5mu\mathsf{T}},\bar{B}^{\mkern-1.5mu\mathsf{T}})^{\mkern-1.5mu\mathsf{T}}=\left(\bar{C}^{\mkern-1.5mu\mathsf{T}}\frac{\partial h_{1}}{\partial A},\bar{C}^{\mkern-1.5mu\mathsf{T}}\frac{\partial h_{1}}{\partial B}\right)^{\mkern-1.5mu\mathsf{T}}. (A.5)

Given the fact that we are dealing with a scalar output variable xx, we recall that C¯\bar{C} can be considered a vector, such that the adjoint function is a vector-Jacobian-product (vJP). We can see that the this maping of the adjoint variables with adjoint functions eventually produces the gradient

∇h=(A¯,B¯)=(∂h1∂A​C¯,∂h1∂B​C¯)=(∂h1∂A​∂h2∂C,∂h1∂B​∂h2∂C).\begin{split}\nabla h=\left(\bar{A},\bar{B}\right)&=\left(\frac{\partial h_{1}}{\partial A}\bar{C},\frac{\partial h_{1}}{\partial B}\bar{C}\right)\\ &=\left(\frac{\partial h_{1}}{\partial A}\frac{\partial h_{2}}{\partial C},\frac{\partial h_{1}}{\partial B}\frac{\partial h_{2}}{\partial C}\right).\end{split} (A.6)

Appendix B Automatic differentiation for complex variables

Some extra attention has to be given to the case in which the primitive functions are complex valued. This is because not all functions one might want to consider are complex-differentiable (holomorphic) and as such the derivative depends on the direction we move in the complex plane when taking the limit for the derivative. In such a case one needs to resort to the calculus of two sets of independent real variables. For a generic function f:C→Cf:\mdmathbb{C}\xrightarrow{}\mdmathbb{C} this can be done by treating xx and yy in z=x+i​yz=x+iy as independent variables or alternatively, by choosing zz and z∗z^{*} and making use of Wirtinger calculus. However we should also note that in the iPEPS use case we deal with a function E:Cn→RE:\mdmathbb{C}^{n}\xrightarrow{}\mdmathbb{R}, which removes the necessity to think about holomorphism.

Appendix C The implicit function theorem and its use at the CTMRG fixed-point

In this section, we are going to present an alternative approach to taking the derivative of the energy function by utilizing the fixed point of the CTMRG procedure. To this end, we can make use of the implicit function theorem [148] to calculate the derivative of the full fixed-point routine. Our discussion will follow the description of Refs. [149, 150]. Differentiating Eq. (17) on both sides we end up with

∂Ae∗​(A)=∂Ac⁡(A,e∗)+∂e∗c⁡(A,e∗)​∂Ae∗​(A).\displaystyle\partial_{A}e^{*}(A)=\partial_{A}c(A,e^{*})+\partial_{e^{*}}c(A,e^{*})\partial_{A}e^{*}(A). (C.1)

Introducing the shorthand writing for the Jacobians L=∂Ac⁡(A,e∗​(A))L=\partial_{A}c(A,e^{*}(A)) and K=∂e∗c⁡(A,e∗​(A))K=\partial_{e^{*}}c(A,e^{*}(A)) and rearranging the equation we find

∂Ae∗​(A)=(L+K​∂Ae∗​(A))=(∑n=0∞K)​L=(𝟙−K)−1​L.\begin{split}\partial_{A}e^{*}(A)=&(L+K\partial_{A}e^{*}(A))\\ =&\left(\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}K\right)L=(\mathds{1}-K)^{-1}L.\end{split} (C.2)

As discussed in Appendix A, we aim at finding the adjoint function of the CTMRG iteration at the fixed point, which is a vector-Jacobian product (vJP) 𝐯𝖳​∂Ae∗​(A)\mathbf{v}^{\mkern-1.5mu\mathsf{T}}\partial_{A}e^{*}(A). Inserting Eq. (C.2) yields

𝐯𝖳​∂e∗​(A)=𝐯𝖳​(𝟙−K)−1​L=𝐰𝖳​L,\displaystyle\mathbf{v}^{\mkern-1.5mu\mathsf{T}}\partial e^{*}(A)=\mathbf{v}^{\mkern-1.5mu\mathsf{T}}(\mathds{1}-K)^{-1}L=\mathbf{w}^{\mkern-1.5mu\mathsf{T}}L, (C.3)

where we have introduced 𝐰𝖳:=𝐯𝖳​(𝟙−K)−1\mathbf{w}^{\mkern-1.5mu\mathsf{T}}:=\mathbf{v}^{\mkern-1.5mu\mathsf{T}}(\mathds{1}-K)^{-1}. The second equality in the equation above can be rearranged into another fixed-point equation

𝐰𝖳=𝐯𝖳+𝐰𝖳​K.\displaystyle\mathbf{w}^{\mkern-1.5mu\mathsf{T}}=\mathbf{v}^{\mkern-1.5mu\mathsf{T}}+\mathbf{w}^{\mkern-1.5mu\mathsf{T}}K. (C.4)

Here 𝐰𝖳​K\mathbf{w}^{\mkern-1.5mu\mathsf{T}}K is another vJP but this time only dependent of the derivative of a single absorption step evaluated at the fixed-point of the CTMRG routine. Solving Eq. (C.4) we can find 𝐰𝖳\mathbf{w}^{\mkern-1.5mu\mathsf{T}} to calculate the vJP of the CTMRG routine from Eq. (C.3). In the end we reduced the naive effort of unrolling the fixed-point iterations to just calculate the derivative of a single CTMRG iteration and another fixed-point iteration which both are much less memory intensive.

Appendix D Automatic differentiation in the language of differential geometry

In order to unify the different frameworks for thinking about forward- and backwards-mode AD, we will briefly introduce a mathematical notation for AD. It also serves to give some more precise meaning to the terms “push-forward” and “pullback”, that are sometimes used in forward- and backwards-mode AD discussions, respectively. For this we first recall the general concept of a push-forward and a pullback for the simple case of functions and distributions. Imagine two functions f:M→Nf:M\xrightarrow{}N and g:N→Rg:N\xrightarrow{}\mdmathbb{R}. The pullback of gg along ff allows us to construct a function f∗​g:M→Rf^{*}g:M\xrightarrow{}\mdmathbb{R} for which the domain of the function gg is “pulled back” to the domain of the function ff. This is done by a simple concatenation of ff and gg

f∗​g​(m⏟∈M)=(g∘f)​(m)=g⁡(f⁡(m)).f^{*}g(\underbrace{m}_{\in M})=(g\circ f)(m)=g(f(m)). (D.1)

This construction can now be used to define a push-forward on the dual objects of the functions under integration. These dual objects are distributions. With a distribution, we can integrate a function

∫M∙�:ℱ⁡(M)→R,f↦∫Mf�,\begin{split}\int_{M}\bullet\penalty\ \mu:&\penalty\ \mathcal{F}(M)\xrightarrow{}\mdmathbb{R},\\ &\penalty\ \penalty\ \penalty\ \penalty\ f\penalty\ \penalty\ \penalty\ \xmapsto{}\int_{M}f\mu,\end{split} (D.2)

where ℱ⁡(M)\mathcal{F}(M) are just the functions on MM and �\mu is the distribution. Given such a distribution on MM we can now integrate functions on MM. The push-forward f∗​�f_{*}\mu of �\mu allows us to integrate functions on NN by defining a distribution that is “pushed forward” to NN. This works as

∫Nh⁡(f∗​�)=:∫M(f∗​h)​�,\int_{N}h(f_{*}\mu)=:\int_{M}(f^{*}h)\mu, (D.3)

where hh is a function on NN.

This type of construction for the pullback and push-forward generalizes to many mathematical objects that have a pairing dual. The relevant mathematical objects for AD are the derivative ∂/∂xi{\partial}/{\partial x_{i}} and its pairing dual, the differential d​xidx_{i}.

It might be useful, beyond the conceptual clarity of this notation, to look at AD in this way because one can easily imagine situations where the intermediate data of a function is restricted by constraints such that the “data-space” becomes geometrically non-trivial. An example could be vectors in Rn\mdmathbb{R}^{n} restricted to unit length or matrices in Mn,mM_{n,m} restricted to be unitary. We note that an optimisation in these situations requires some additional concepts, like finding a path on the given space from a tangent vector. This requires some extra care and is not discussed here.

We now introduce the mathematical notation that we need in order to talk about AD in this language. We will not be particularly rigorous in this endeavour and leave out all details that are not explicitly needed. We start with a manifold MM on which we can consider points p∈Mp\in M, as well as functions f:M→Rf:M\xrightarrow{}\mdmathbb{R}. For each point p∈Mp\in M we can define a vector space Tp​MT_{p}M (call it the tangent-space at pp) of tangent-vectors at that point. The elements in Tp​MT_{p}M act like derivatives on functions on MM

e.g.:∂∂xi=ei∈TpM,∂∂xi(f)=∂f∂xi.\text{e.g.:}\penalty\ \penalty\ \penalty\ \frac{\partial}{\partial x_{i}}=e_{i}\in T_{p}M,\penalty\ \penalty\ \penalty\ \frac{\partial}{\partial x_{i}}(f)=\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_{i}}.

Here we have assumed that we have equipped the manifold MM with coordinates via a chart �:M→Rm\phi:M\xrightarrow{}\mdmathbb{R}^{m} around the point p, where m=dim(M)m=\dim(M). Our tangent-space Tp​MT_{p}M has dimension mm and we can choose a canonical basis

{∂∂xi,…,∂∂xm}={e1,…,em}.\left\{\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{i}},\dots,\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{m}}\right\}=\{e_{1},\dots,e_{m}\}.

One further defines the dual vector space Tp∗​MT^{*}_{p}M of the tangent vector space, called cotangent-space. This cotangent-space contains the dual vectors to the derivatives ∂∂xi\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{i}}. These cotangent vectors from the cotangent-space are the differentials d​xidx_{i}. The cotangent-space also has dimension mm and we can choose the canonical basis

{d​x1,…,d​xm}.\{dx_{1},\dots,dx_{m}\}.

Obviously, given the canonical basis for the tangent-space and cotangent-space we can expand arbitrary vectors in these spaces in the basis. Take v∈Tp​Mv\in T_{p}M and d​f∈Tp∗​Mdf\in T^{*}_{p}M we can expand as

v\displaystyle v =∑ivi​∂∂xi=∑ivi​ei,\displaystyle=\sum_{i}v_{i}\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{i}}=\sum_{i}v_{i}e_{i}, (D.4)
d​f\displaystyle df =∑i∂f∂xi​d​xi.\displaystyle=\sum_{i}\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_{i}}dx_{i}. (D.5)

We have a pairing between the derivatives that live in the tangent-space Tp​MT_{p}M and the differentials that live in Tp∗​MT^{*}_{p}M as

d​xj​(∂∂xi):=∂xj∂xi=�i,j.dx_{j}\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{i}}\right):=\frac{\partial x_{j}}{\partial x_{i}}=\delta_{i,j}. (D.6)

Note that by this pairing relation we see that tangent and cotangent vectors are “pairing duals” and we can use an analogous construction for pullbacks and push-forwards as we did for functions and distribution above. Since Tp​MT_{p}M and Tp∗​MT^{*}_{p}M are isomorphic, we can introduce a correspondence transformation between the canonical basis of the two spaces

∙♭\displaystyle\bullet^{\flat} :Tp​M→Tp∗​M,ei↦d​xi=ei♭,\displaystyle:T_{p}M\xrightarrow{}T_{p}^{*}M,\penalty\ \penalty\ \penalty\ e_{i}\xmapsto{}dx_{i}=e_{i}^{\flat}, (D.7)
∙♯\displaystyle\bullet^{\sharp} :Tp∗​M→Tp​M,d​xi↦ei=d​xi♯.\displaystyle:T^{*}_{p}M\xrightarrow{}T_{p}M,\penalty\ \penalty\ \penalty\ dx_{i}\xmapsto{}e_{i}=dx_{i}^{\sharp}. (D.8)

We now have assembled all nessessary tools to formulate what a “gradient” is in this language. It is given by

∇f:=(d​f)♯,\nabla f:=(df)^{\sharp}, (D.9)

which matches the common formula

∇f=(∑i∂f∂xi​d​xi)♯=∑i∂f∂xi​ei=(∂f∂x1,…,∂f∂xm),\begin{split}\nabla f=\left(\sum_{i}\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_{i}}dx_{i}\right)^{\sharp}&=\sum_{i}\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_{i}}e_{i}\\ &=\left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_{1}},\dots,\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_{m}}\right),\end{split} (D.10)

where we have taken eie_{i} just as the ii-th unit vector of Tp​MT_{p}M.

Now it is easy to construct the pullbacks and push-forwards in this context analogous to our treatment of functions and distributions. For this we start from manifolds MM and NN with points p∈Mp\in M and q∈Nq\in N, and with the two functions f:M→Nf:M\xrightarrow{}N and g:N→Rg:N\xrightarrow{}\mdmathbb{R}. We can consider a differential d​g∈Tq∗​Ndg\in T_{q}^{*}N which we want to “pull back” along the function ff and associate it with and element of Tf−1​(q)∗​MT_{f^{-1}(q)}^{*}M, where f−1​(q)∈Mf^{-1}(q)\in M. We do this with the familiar definition

f∗​d​g⏟∈Tf−1​(q)∗​M:=d⁡(g∘f)\underbrace{f^{*}dg}_{\in T^{*}_{f^{-1}(q)}M}:=d(g\circ f) (D.11)

which uses a concatenation of ff and gg just as in the first example. For a tangible example consider g=xig=x_{i} to be a coordinate function. We then get f∗​d​xi=d⁡(xi∘f)=d⁡(fi)f^{*}dx_{i}=d(x_{i}\circ f)=d(f_{i}). As before the push-forward can be defined via the pullback just as we had done for functions and distributions. In this case, we start with a tangent vector ∂∂xi\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{i}} in Tp​MT_{p}M and want to “push it forward” along ff into Tf⁡(p)​NT_{f(p)}N. This works as

(f∗​(∂∂xi⏞∈Tp​M)⏟∈Tf⁡(p)​N)​(g):=∂∂xi​(f∗​g)=∂∂xi​(g∘f).(\underbrace{f_{*}\biggl(\overbrace{\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{i}}}^{\in T_{p}M}\biggr)}_{\in T_{f(p)}N})(g):=\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{i}}(f^{*}g)=\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{i}}(g\circ f). (D.12)

Now that we are equipped with the pullback and push-forward of differentials and derivatives we see how the gradient is calculated in the forward- and backward-mode AD. For this we will go back to our neat example from Sec. 2.4 and slightly generalize. Say, we would like to take the gradient ∇E\nabla E of a function that is composed of three primitive functions E=f3∘f2∘f1E=f_{3}\circ f_{2}\circ f_{1}. We say these primitive functions map between manifolds

E:M1↦f1M2↦f2M3↦f3R.E:M_{1}\xmapsto{f_{1}}M_{2}\xmapsto{f_{2}}M_{3}\xmapsto{f_{3}}\mdmathbb{R}. (D.13)

Lets first look at what happens when we build the gradient using backwards-mode AD. In this case we start with the differential d​f3df_{3} of the last primary function of EE. This differential lives in Tk∗​M3T^{*}_{k}M_{3}, where k∈M3k\in M_{3} is a point in M3M_{3}. We can now use the pullback along the functions f2f_{2} and then f1f_{1} to pull back this differential to M1M_{1}

f1∗​(f2∗​(d​f3))←pullbackf2∗​(d​f3)←pullbackd​f3.f_{1}^{*}(f_{2}^{*}(df_{3}))\xleftarrow{\text{pullback}}f_{2}^{*}(df_{3})\xleftarrow{\text{pullback}}df_{3}. (D.14)

With the definitions above we see that in this way we construct the gradient

f1∗​(f2∗​(d​f3))=f1∗​((d⁡(f3∘f2)))=d⁡(f3∘f2∘f1)=d​E.f_{1}^{*}(f_{2}^{*}(df_{3}))=f_{1}^{*}((d(f_{3}\circ f_{2})))=d(f_{3}\circ f_{2}\circ f_{1})=dE. (D.15)

With our identification between tangent and cotangent vectors we finalize to ∇E=(d​E)♯\nabla E=\left(dE\right)^{\sharp}. If we express the differential that we start from d​f3df_{3} in coordinates, we straightforwardly obtain the product of Jacobians as a result for the gradient. This also establishes the connection to the adjoint functions we talked about in the previous section and the vector-Jacobian product as discussed in Sec. 2.4.

In the case of forward-mode AD we start from a tangent vector ∂∂xi\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{i}}, which lives in Tl​M1T_{l}M_{1}, where l∈M1l\in M_{1} is a point in M1M_{1}. We can now push this tangent vector forward into a tangent space of M3M_{3} with successive push-forwards along f1f_{1} followed by f2f_{2}

∂∂xi→push-forwardf1∗(∂∂xi)→push-forwardf2∗(f1∗(∂∂xi)).\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{i}}\xrightarrow{\text{push-forward}}f_{1*}\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{i}}\right)\xrightarrow{\text{push-forward}}f_{2*}\left(f_{1*}\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{i}}\right)\right). (D.16)

With the definitions for the push-forward we see that the gradient we obtain in this way is given by

∑if2∗(f1∗(∂∂xi))(f3)ei=∑if1∗(∂∂xi)(f3∘f2)ei=∑i∂∂xi​(f3∘f2∘f1⏟=E)​ei=∇E.\begin{split}\sum_{i}f_{2*}\left(f_{1*}\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{i}}\right)\right)(f_{3})\penalty\ e_{i}&=\sum_{i}f_{1*}\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{i}}\right)(f_{3}\circ f_{2})\penalty\ e_{i}\\ &=\sum_{i}\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{i}}(\underbrace{f_{3}\circ f_{2}\circ f_{1}}_{=E})\penalty\ e_{i}\\ &=\nabla E.\end{split} (D.17)
